analysis.one_liner: Requires every home mortgage application to be logged in a national clearinghouse to catch fraud and redlining.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in late July 2010, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and died there without a single cosponsor or committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for any lender to extend a mortgage secured by a one-to-four family home unless the original application is first recorded in a national clearinghouse. The clearinghouse, run by a private contractor overseen by Treasury's financial-crimes unit, would give every application a unique ID and collect who applied, who took the application, which lenders saw it, and what kind of loan resulted. Federal and state regulators and law enforcement would have access to the full dataset, giving them a way to spot mortgage fraud and discriminatory lending (redlining) that today leaves no central trail.
analysis.who_benefits: Home loan applicants, especially borrowers in neighborhoods where lenders historically refused to lend or steered people into bad loans. A central record of every application would let regulators and law enforcement detect fraud, discrimination, and predatory practices across lenders, and would show which lenders saw an application and declined it.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to extend mortgage credit secured by a one-to-four family residence unless the application is recorded with the clearinghouse at the time it is first received [S3].

Gives the Treasury Secretary, acting through FinCEN, access to all collected data for the purpose of investigating fraudulent, discriminatory, or predatory activities, and gives state regulators and law enforcement access as well [S3].

Records which lenders received an application and which accepted it, and whether the property is a principal residence or investment property, creating a data trail for detecting redlining and loan flipping [S3].
Requires applicants to receive a written disclosure about what information is collected, who can access it, and how it may be used [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage originators, who would pay a per-application fee sized to cover the clearinghouse's costs plus a market rate of return, a cost likely passed on to borrowers in loan pricing. Applicants would also have their name, Social Security number, and property details stored in a national database.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage lenders, and borrowers via fees

drawbacks.text: The clearinghouse would collect every applicant's name, Social Security number, and address in a single internet-based national database, creating a large honeypot of sensitive financial data whose security depends on regulations the Secretary would write later [S3].

The clearinghouse would be run by a private contractor whose startup and operating costs could be backstopped by a Treasury guarantee of repayment on its loan, putting federal credit behind a private monopoly on mortgage application data [S3].
Per-application fees on originators would be recovered through loan pricing, so ordinary borrowers would ultimately bear the cost of the system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is a real fraud- and discrimination-fighting tool: mortgage applications today leave no central record of who applied, who shopped, and who was turned down, which is exactly the information needed to prove redlining or catch serial fraud. The costs are the privacy risk of a national database of Social Security numbers, the fees passed to borrowers, and the design choice to hand the system to a private small-business contractor backstopped by a Treasury guarantee rather than run it in-house. On balance a defensible consumer-protection bill, though its practical value depends entirely on regulations never written because the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 29, 2010 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which took no further action before the Congress ended in January 2011; no cosponsor ever signed on and no vote was ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Edolphus Towns introduced the bill in the House on July 29, 2010 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, the only committee action it ever received [S5].
No further action, no markup, and no floor vote occurred before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage originators avoided a per-application recordation requirement and fee, and avoided a national dataset that regulators could use for redlining and fraud enforcement. Borrowers gained nothing because the system was never built.

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee, where he was a member as chairman of the Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill after referral; no markup, no report, no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough engagement to reveal a partisan pattern: it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would require every mortgage application to be recorded in a national clearinghouse, with per-application fees on originators and full regulator access to the data. That transparency directly serves borrowers and law enforcement hunting fraud and redlining, which is why lenders bear the cost and lose information control.

industries.industry: Mortgage application data services (prospective clearinghouse contractor)
industries.note: The bill would create a new private franchise: one small-business contractor would run the national clearinghouse, charge originators fees, and have its startup loan guaranteed by Treasury. A real business opportunity, though required to be independent of the mortgage industry.
